Based on TACE clinical guidelines, we set
up the exploration configurations, including all potential
chemotherapy drugs ( e.g., Raltitrexed, Cisplatin) and em-
bolism materials (e.g., Lipiodol, Gelatin Sponge). The two
parts constitute the action base, which provides possible
TACE protocols for Generative Dynamics Models as condi-
tions. Then, we adopt a pre-trained large multimodal model
(LMM), e.g., GPT-4o, to serve as policies. Given a high-
level goal g (e.g., “What TACE treatment protocols are rec-
ommended for a patient diagnosed with hepatocellular car-
cinoma (HCC) given the pre-treatment CT?”), the policy
model πVLM(x0, g) extracts the visual observation and tu-
mor context from the given pre-treatment CT x0 to prompt
the proper Transarterial Chemoembolization (TACE) ac-
tions. To constrain the excessively large tree search in the
action base, we further prompt the Large Language Reason-
ing Model, i.e., Deepseek-R1 [22], to refine the drug set and
embolism set by the clinical policies, whose final cardinali-
ties are D and E, respectively.

most existing studies focus on human-authored radiology
reports, we aim to address radiotherapy reports to extract
more comprehensive information on treatment protocols.

der controlled tumor synthesis. To mitigate these issues, we

Heuristic Function. We use survival analysis model
to implement a heuristic function Hsurv(x0, m0, ˆx, m0, g),
which quantifies the efficacy under the specific TACE action
combo by the output risk score. Inspired by DeepSurv [35],
we utilize a 3D convolution-based model structure, the 3D
ResNet (MC3) [58], as the feature extractor of survival anal-
ysis model. Given the pre-treatment pair (x0, m0) and sim-
ulated post-treatment pair (ˆx, ˆm), we extract their concate-
nated CT and mask, respectively, and bidirectionally align
the semantics of pre- and post-treatment by Cross-Attention
Transformer [37]. After that, we adopt an attention-based
aggregator to fuse pre- and post-features, followed by fc
layers to determine the risk score. The action combo with
a lower risk score should bring greater efficacy for the pa-
tient. Note that, for training, we leverage multi-task learn-
ing strategy,i.e., CoxPH [35] and OS regression, to improve
the generalization of survival analysis.

With this objective in mind, we exhibit a tree-search ex-
ploration procedure. Our exploration algorithm initializes a
set of B parallel protocol beams. We sample the potential
action space composed of D drugs and E embolisms and
clinical rules using πVLM. The clinical rules are introduced
to prune unreasonable branches, e.g., concomitant use of
multiple platinum-based agents is contraindicated due to the
risk of cumulative toxicity and myelosuppression. We se-
quentially explore the two parts to ensure that TACE pro-
tocol contains both drugs and embolism. For each current
action combo, we synthesize T post-treatment tumors from
fDM(x0, m0, a) to obtain a more reliable simulation. We
then use our heuristic function Hsurv(x0, m0, ˆx, ˆm, g) with
the assistance of Hseg(ˆx) to select the generated tumor with
the best average survival score of T replicas among D or E
actions. After every step of extending all beams, we discard
the beam with the worst survival score and replace its ac-
tion combo with the best beam. To prevent cumulative toxi-
city and organ dysfunction, we prohibit over-exploration by

Visual Turing Test (Human Evaluation). We conduct
an action-driven Visual Turing Test on 240 CT scans of
post-treatment tumors, where 120 scans contain real post-
treatment tumors, and 120 scans contain synthetic post-
treatment tumors generated by different tumor synthesis
models. Three radiologists (R1-R3) participated in this
study, independently evaluating five groups of 48 CT scans
each and classifying them as either real or synthetic. It
is important to note that the radiologists’ evaluations are
based on whether the synthetic tumor closely resembles a
post-treatment tumor, which typically contains a mixture of
lipiodol deposition, necrotic, and viable tumor regions, dis-
tinguishing it from ordinary pre-treatment tumors. The test
results are summarized in Table 1. The sensitivity scores
of all radiologists remain high (above 91%), demonstrating
their ability to correctly identify real post-treatment tumors.
However, specificity scores vary among the methods, in-
dicating different levels of realism in the synthetic tumors.
Notably, our method MeWM achieves the lowest specificity
scores (79.17% for R1, 70.83% for R2, and 75.00% for R3),
suggesting that a large proportion of synthetic tumors gen-
erated by our approach are mistaken as real. This indicates
superior realism compared to other methods such as Syn-
Tumor [30], Pixel2Cancer [38], DiffTumor [11], and Tex-
toMorph [43]. Figure 4 illustrates examples from the test

evidence_fragments.content:
MeWM as A Clinical Decision-support Tool. MeWM
demonstrates significant potential in augmenting the ca-
pabilities of radiologists and physicians, underscoring its
clinical relevance in optimizing TACE planning. Reliance
solely on pre-treatment CT often results in partial ob-
servation and suboptimal targeting due to heterogeneous
pathological conditions. By incorporating MeWM’s rec-
ommended protocol, clinical decision-making is markedly
enhanced, yielding performance improvements of 12.70,
11.45, 14.22, and 10.77 in F1-score, Jaccard, Precision,
and Recall on our dataset. MeWM facilitates accurate tu-
mor localization and enables predictive assessment of post-
embolization outcomes, thereby reducing procedural uncer-
tainty. Moreover, its synthetic post-treatment CT projec-
tions help anticipate embolization efficacy, optimize TACE
distribution, and mitigate non-target embolization risks,
contributing to enhanced therapeutic precision and individ-
ualized strategies. MeWM serves as a critical decision-
support tool in interventional oncology, bridging anatomi-
cal imaging with functional assessment for meaningful clin-
ical outcomes. As shown in Figure 7, interventional physi-
cians refine TACE protocols by MeWM intervention, align-
ing treatment with expert practices.

capability_assessments.rationale: Learned CT-to-post-treatment tumor dynamics condition on TACE combinations. A guideline-constrained beam optimizer scores generated outcomes with segmentation/survival models. L4 is offline protocol-agreement evaluation of an actual optimizer, not improved patient survival or identified treatment effects.

gate_assessments.rationale: Data availability, leakage and source split assumptions require audit; no gate pass inferred.

legacy_cells.C: Yijun Yang, Zhao-Yang Wang, Qiuping Liu, Shuwen Sun, Kang Wang, Rama Chellappa, et al.
legacy_cells.O: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) / liver tumors treated with TACE
legacy_cells.S: Which TACE drug and embolization protocol should be selected for an HCC patient, based on simulated post-treatment tumor CT and survival-risk scoring?
legacy_cells.T: HCC patients treated with TACE; the in-house dataset contains 338 longitudinal paired pre- and post-treatment CT scans.
legacy_cells.V: Select a patient-specific TACE protocol comprising drug and embolism components.
legacy_cells.AI: 3D pre-treatment and post-treatment CT volumes; tumor masks; textual treatment-action descriptions and radiotherapy reports
legacy_cells.AJ: 3D VQGAN autoencoder for CT latent encoding; 3D U-Net diffusion denoiser; CLIP text encoder; adapted nnU-Net segmentation model
legacy_cells.AM: Action text and learnable concept embeddings are concatenated and projected; action embeddings condition the diffusion model together with masked pre-treatment CT latent features.
legacy_cells.BD: Drug and embolism components; radiotherapy-report preprocessing extracts drugs, embolic agents, and corresponding dosages.
legacy_cells.BF: Clinical-rule pruning includes a contraindication against concomitant use of multiple platinum-based agents due to cumulative toxicity and myelosuppression.
legacy_cells.BS: Synthetic post-treatment CT volumes/tumors; a segmentation model predicts post-treatment liver and tumor masks for survival-risk analysis.
legacy_cells.BT: Survival-risk score from pre-treatment and simulated post-treatment CT/masks, using a survival-analysis model.
legacy_cells.BU: Minimize the survival-model risk score for the simulated post-treatment result; lower risk is treated as greater efficacy.
legacy_cells.BV: Diffusion denoising noise-prediction loss; combo-contrastive loss; CoxPH and overall-survival regression multitask objectives for the survival model.
legacy_cells.CK: Search drug and embolism actions by simulating post-treatment tumors and scoring them with the survival-risk heuristic; clinical rules prune contraindicated combinations.
legacy_cells.EE: Three radiologists independently classified 240 real/synthetic post-treatment CT scans in a visual Turing test. A separate interventional-physician treatment-selection assistance study reports improved F1.
legacy_cells.EF: 3 radiologists in the visual Turing test; see separate physician-assistance experiment for its participant count.
legacy_cells.FN: Reported results (source excerpt): Notably, MeWM improves clinical decision-making for interventional physicians, boosting F1-score in selecting the optimal TACE protocol by 13%, paving the way for future integration of medical world models as the second readers.
legacy_cells.FS: Reviewer mapping: M3 Belief-state service; M4 Action service; M5 Dynamics adapter; M7 Outcome & causal layer; M8 Planner; M9 Safety & governance
legacy_cells.FT: Reviewer lesson: Keep the learned patient/scene simulator separate from the planner objective; constrain candidate actions and report closed-loop decision quality alongside model fidelity.
legacy_cells.FX: Title and abstract (PDF p. 1); Introduction and related work (pp. 1–3); Methods, including policy, dynamics, inverse dynamics, algorithm and model details (pp. 3–6); Experiments and dataset descriptions (p. 6); Results and Tables 1–3 covering generation quality, survival analysis, and TACE protocol exploration (pp. 6–8); Conclusion (p. 8). The extracted paper has no separate limitations section; acknowledgements and references were inspected through p. 11. | Codex audit: title/byline, abstract/conclusion, targeted methods/results and cross-check of prior quotations against extracted full text. This is a targeted audit, not an independent re-extraction of every negative/unreported field.
legacy_cells.FZ: A:I were left untouched because the PDF did not directly contradict the prefilled metadata. No explicit causal identification strategy or assumptions are reported, so treatment-conditioned predictions are classified as associational. Tables 1–3 are present, but portions of their extracted text have interleaved or shifted columns; no table-dependent numerical result is transcribed. The paper provides retrospective dataset-based evaluations, not prospective clinical readiness evidence. No separate limitations section was found in the extracted paper. Evidence QA: 15/43 populated fields had a <=25-word quotation matching extracted PDF text (34.9%). Confidence is conservative; review this row where exact quote checks were incomplete. Codex audit: 34 prior populated fields have a located source quotation; 9 have quotations not located by normalized text matching. Unlocated quotations are review flags, not proof that the value is false. Companion evidence audit lists affected columns. Reviewer FS/FT/FU mappings are synthesis. Prior unsupported/missing fields remain Not reported; no clinical benefit inferred from offline simulation.

limitations: Public cohort is 80% fine-tuned/validated and20% tested; not untouched external validation.
Training attenuation is derived from report-described occlusion effects; availability/leakage implications unresolved.
Gold-action agreement and modeled survival are proxies; no prospective therapeutic execution or measured survival improvement.
Code URL identified but repository version/access/license not inspected.
One automated Codex source-review pass with skeptical criterion check; no independent human review or experimental reproduction.
Source references/bibliography were read as entries, not retrieved as independent primary studies.
Schema/quote occurrence checks are necessary checks, not proof of clinical safety, causal identification or complete scientific correctness.
